job.style: a description of a classroom activity or experiment and what it shows

passage: In our Social Science class, we simulated a state election to understand how government works. Our teacher explained that a state is divided into specific geographical areas called constituencies, which are not the same as administrative districts. Each constituency elects one representative to the Legislative Assembly, known as an MLA. During our activity, we learned that a party needs more than half of the total seats in the assembly to form the government, which is called a majority. If there are 100 seats, a party needs at least 51 to win. We also discussed that the Chief Minister is not directly chosen by the public. Instead, the MLAs belonging to the winning party elect their leader, who is then appointed by the Governor as the Chief Minister. This process ensures that the executive branch is formed by those who have the support of the elected representatives. By mapping out these roles, we saw that the government is a team effort rather than the result of a single person's popularity or a simple district-based count. This activity clarified that winning the most seats is not enough if it does not cross the majority threshold, and that the Chief Minister's position is a result of internal party selection.

items.evidence: During our activity, we learned that a party needs more than half of the total seats in the assembly to form the government, which is called a majority.
items.q: A state assembly has 200 seats. How many must one party win to form the government alone?
options: At least 101 seats
At least 100 seats
At least 51 seats
At least 102 seats
items.explain: A majority means more than half; half of 200 is 100, so 101 seats are needed.

wrong.why: thinks exactly half is enough for a majority
copies the number 51 from the 100-seat example
doubles 51 instead of finding more than half

items.evidence: This activity clarified that winning the most seats is not enough if it does not cross the majority threshold, and that the Chief Minister's position is a result of internal party selection.
items.q: Party A wins 45 of 100 seats, the most of any party. Why can't it rule alone?
options: It has not crossed the halfway mark of 50
It did not get the most votes overall
Its leader was not chosen by the voters
It did not win in every single district
items.explain: Winning the most seats is not enough; a party must cross half, here more than 50.

wrong.why: thinks majority means the most votes
thinks the people directly elect the Chief Minister
thinks constituencies are the same as districts

items.evidence: Instead, the MLAs belonging to the winning party elect their leader, who is then appointed by the Governor as the Chief Minister.
items.q: How does someone become Chief Minister after a state election?
options: Winning party's MLAs choose; the Governor then appoints
Voters of the state choose; the Governor then announces
The Governor chooses; the winning MLAs then agree
Top vote-getting MLA wins; the Governor then announces
items.explain: MLAs of the winning party elect their leader, and the Governor appoints that leader as Chief Minister.

wrong.why: thinks the people elect the Chief Minister directly
thinks the Governor picks the ruling party's leader
thinks most votes decides the post

items.evidence: Each constituency elects one representative to the Legislative Assembly, known as an MLA.
items.q: Why is a state divided into constituencies before an election?
options: So each area sends one MLA to the Assembly
So each district can collect its own taxes
So each area can elect the Chief Minister
So each area gets an MLA from the ruling party
items.explain: Each constituency elects one representative, called an MLA, to the Legislative Assembly.

wrong.why: thinks people vote directly for the Chief Minister
thinks every MLA belongs to the ruling party

items.evidence: By mapping out these roles, we saw that the government is a team effort rather than the result of a single person's popularity or a simple district-based count.
items.q: The class called the state government a team effort. Which idea explains this?
options: Power rests on the backing of many MLAs
Power rests on one leader's popularity alone
Power rests on counting districts each party wins
Power rests on the Governor's own party choice
items.explain: Government is a team effort built on support of elected MLAs, not one person's popularity or district counts.

wrong.why: reverses the passage, which rejects single-person popularity
thinks seats are counted by districts
thinks the Governor belongs to and picks the ruling party
